The abomination in that temple
The desolation was tied to the very stones he said would fall. Missing this is why many feel they must invent a third temple.
The warning was local: those in Judea were to run to the mountains. No one on the other side of the world was told to prepare.
This generation

Early Christians remembered the warning and left for Pella, across the Jordan, before the siege. Those who heeded Christ escaped.
“Your companion in the tribulation”
John was already sharing in the tribulation he wrote about; it was not thousands of years away.
Seven real churches
The book was sent to congregations of John’s day, who were expected to read it, understand it and keep it.
Shortly; the time is near
The opening and closing verses stress that these things must soon take place.
The dragon thrown down
The dragon falls after the child is born and caught up to God’s throne: Christ’s first coming, cross and ascension.
Five fallen, one is
When John wrote, five kings had fallen, one was reigning, and one would come for a little while. The prophecy sits in his own day.
The city that rules the kings
For John’s readers, the great city reigning over the kings of the earth pointed to Rome.
Many partial preterists see the harlot as Jerusalem, the city “where their Lord was crucified” (11:8), riding the Roman beast.
One reading: Christ conquers the old pagan world with the sword from his mouth, the word of God, until Rome bows and the gospel fills the empire.
Many read it as the second coming; others as Christ’s judgement in AD 70.
Satan bound, Christ reigning, and the martyrs on thrones with him. The text places their thrones with Christ, not on earth.
After the thousand years
The part still future to John: Christ’s bodily return and the final judgement.
God dwells with his people for ever, and his glory makes the sun unnecessary.
Many see the new creation begun already in Christ and the church, and completed at the end.

Why Matthew 24 and most of Revelation lie in the past
Were Matthew 24 and Revelation written about a far-off future, or about events their first readers would live through?
The temple in front of them
Jesus said not one stone of the temple his disciples were admiring would be left on another: the Second Temple, not a future one.
Local, specific, timed
Those in Judea were to flee to the mountains, and all these things would happen within that generation.
Heeded and fulfilled
The early church fled to Pella before the siege; Jerusalem and its temple fell in AD 70. The abomination belonged to that temple, so no third temple is needed.
Revelation's first readers
John was already their companion in the tribulation, writing to seven real churches about things that must soon take place, for the time was near.
Rooted in John's day
The dragon falls after Christ's ascension. Of the seven kings, five had fallen and one was reigning as John wrote. The great city ruled the kings of the earth in his day.
The rider and the reign
The rider conquers by the sword from his mouth, the word of God; then Christ reigns with his martyrs through the thousand years.
What lay far ahead
Only what follows the thousand years was distant: Christ's bodily return, the final judgement and the New Jerusalem where God dwells with his people.

Futurists answer that Revelation was written about AD 95, after the temple fell; that “soon” describes the manner or certainty of events; and that the rider of Revelation 19 is plainly Christ's visible second coming, since he comes from an opened heaven with the armies of heaven.

The audience, the setting and the time words point to the first century. Most of Matthew 24 and Revelation was fulfilled then, Christ reigns now, and his return, the judgement and the new creation are still ahead.

Readers who share this view still differ on details: many partial preterists see the harlot as Jerusalem rather than Rome, and many read Revelation 19 as Christ's coming in judgement in AD 70, or as his final return. The date of Revelation is debated; see the dating study.
